subtopicTitle: Orbital perturbations — J2 effect (oblateness), derivation of nodal precession

cards.front: Define the dimensionless J2 zonal harmonic coefficient and its physical origin.
cards.back: J2 = (C−A)/(M R_e²) where C>A are principal moments of inertia; it quantifies Earth's oblateness (equatorial bulge) in the gravitational potential expansion V = −(μ/r)[1 − Σ J_n (R_e/r)^n P_n(sin φ)].

cards.front: What orbital element experiences secular drift due to J2 and why?
cards.back: Right ascension of ascending node Ω precesses because the equatorial bulge produces a torque that rotates the orbital plane about Earth's polar axis; inclination i remains constant to first order.

cards.front: Write the standard expression for mean-motion nodal precession rate Ω̇ due to J2.
cards.back: Ω̇ = −(3/2) n J2 (R_e/a)² cos i / (1−e²)² where n=√(μ/a³) is mean motion.

cards.front: State the two key assumptions used when averaging the J2 disturbing function over one orbital period.
cards.back: (1) Orbit is Keplerian to zeroth order; (2) average is taken over mean anomaly M while holding a,e,i fixed (short-period terms vanish).

cards.front: For a circular low-Earth orbit at a=7000 km, i=98°, compute the approximate nodal precession period (J2=1.0826e−3, R_e=6378 km).
Derive the factor (3/2)cos i that appears in Ω̇ from the averaged J2 potential R_J2.
cards.back: R_J2 = (μ J2 R_e²/(2a³(1−e²)^{3/2}))(3/2 sin²i −1); ∂R/∂h (h=angular momentum) yields Ω̇ = (1/(n a² √(1−e²) sin i)) ∂R/∂i giving the (3/2)cos i term after differentiation.

cards.front: What inclination satisfies Ω̇ = (2π/365.25) rad/day for a sun-synchronous orbit?
cards.back: i_ss ≈ 98.43° ( retrograde, near-polar) for typical LEO altitudes; solves cos i = −(2/3) (a/R_e)² (1−e²)² (n/J2) (365.25/2π).
